newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Dutch EU presidency sees difficult times ahead.
newsitem.headline: Dutch EU presidency sees difficult times ahead.

text.p: The Netherlands said on Wednesday its presidency of the European Union would sound a sober note in its race to agree key institutional reforms ahead of the planned enlargement of the 15-member alliance.

In a low-key presentation of the Dutch plans, Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said they would not press a 'wish list' of national concerns but would build on the work of the outgoing Irish presidency in a bid to agree a substantial successor to the Maastricht Treaty.
"We will take (Ireland's work) further...It is what I would call a sober note, sobriety in difficult times," Van Mierlo said.
"The agenda for Europe has so much on it that there is really no room left for specific desiderata of our own," he told a news conference.

The Dutch presidency, which begins on January 1, is charged with rounding off the 18-month intergovernmental conference (IGC) reviewing the EU treaty finalised under the previous Dutch presidency in 1991.

Key issues that need to be resolved include the introduction of qualified majority voting in several areas which currently still demand unanimous decision-making, the composition of the European Commission and Council of Ministers in an enlarged Union, and greater powers for the European parliament.
On a separate front, the Dutch presidency must also oversee further preparations for monetary union.

It will be required to hammer out the details of the stability pact for sustained budgetary discipline agreed by member states in Dublin last week and to lead negotiations on a revamped Euro-linked exchange rate mechanism.
In addition it will oversee the follow-up to the Barcelona Conference on closer relations between the EU and Mediterranean countries, due to be held in April, and seek to bolster transatlantic ties.
But Van Mierlo said that agreement on a revised "Treaty of Amsterdam" could well still be jeopardised by British Euroscepticism.
"If the United Kingdom maintains all its current positions then there is not much chance of a substantive treaty," he said.
"We are pinning our hopes on some room for negotiation after the (British) elections," he added.
